answer: Not quite: the King James Bible says "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10) [1], and the World English Bible renders it "a root of all kinds of evil" [2]. Whether the verse means all evil or all kinds of evil is a matter of translation debate [3].

Nobody knows: the author of Beowulf is anonymous, and scholars call him the "Beowulf poet" [1]. Its date is also disputed; Leonard Neidorf and others argue it was the work of a single author in the late 7th or early 8th century, though other scholars disagree [3][6].

Besides Pride and Prejudice and Emma, Jane Austen wrote Sense and Sensibility (1811) and Mansfield Park (1814), and two novels published after her death in 1817, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion [1]. She also began Sanditon, which was left unfinished when she died [1].
Mary Shelley was 20 when Frankenstein came out: she was born on 30 August 1797 [1] and the novel was published on 1 January 1818 [4], about four months before her 21st birthday.
No. Jane Austen died on 18 July 1817 [4], and Frankenstein was first published on 1 January 1818, about six months later [3].
Neither: Charles Darwin and Abraham Lincoln were born on the same day, 12 February 1809 [1][3][4]. Darwin lived longer, dying on 19 April 1882, while Lincoln was assassinated on 15 April 1865 [3][4].
The passages name Alexander's own teacher, the philosopher Aristotle, who tutored him until he was 16 [1][2], but they don't say who taught Aristotle.
The author, Gabriel García Márquez, was Colombian [1], but the passages don't name Colombia's capital.

The Mayflower carried the Pilgrims to the New World in 1620 [1], but the passages don't give the year Columbus first reached the Americas; they only mention his later voyages of 1493, 1498 and 1502 [3], so the gap can't be worked out from them.
213 years: the Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776 [4], and the East German government opened the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989 [1].
About 22 years: On the Origin of Species was published on 24 November 1859 [5], and Darwin died on 19 April 1882 [1], twenty-two years and five months later.
Not overall: the Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world but the third-largest desert, smaller than the deserts of Antarctica and the Arctic [1][2].

Yes, in several places. One is the verse "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise" (20:1) in the King James Bible [4]. More broadly, the Bible treats wine both as a blessing and as a danger, personifying it as a mocker and condemning drunkenness in many passages [1][2].

The apostle Paul: the letter opens "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle" [1]. Scholars agree Paul composed it, probably in Corinth around AD 55 to 57, with Tertius transcribing it as his amanuensis [2][3].

Yes: Matthew 6:34 in the King James Bible reads "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself" [2]. The Berean Standard Bible has it as "do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself" [3][4].

Not quite: the King James Bible says "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1 Timothy 6:10) [4]. The World English Bible renders it "a root of all kinds of evil" [1], and which reading is right is debated [2].
Daniel: the king commanded "and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions" (6:16) [1][2]. He was taken out unhurt, and his accusers were thrown in instead [4].

Love them: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you" (5:44) [3]. The verse is part of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew [1].
Yes: the King James Bible commands "Ye shall not make any cuttings in your flesh for the dead, nor print any marks upon you: I am the LORD" (19:28) [4].

Treat them as your own people: "if a stranger sojourn with thee in your land, ye shall not vex him", and "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt" (19:33-34) [4]. Other verses give the sojourner the same law as the native and a share of the harvest (Leviticus 24:22, Exodus 12:49, Deuteronomy 24:19-21) [1][2].

Yes. Asked whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar, Jesus said "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's" (22:21) [3]. The Berean and World English Bibles tell the same episode as a question about paying taxes to Caesar [2][4].

Yes. In his first soliloquy Hamlet wishes his "too too solid flesh would melt, thaw, and resolve itself into a dew", or that "the Everlasting had not fix'd his canon 'gainst self-slaughter" [4], meaning he would end his life if God had not forbidden it.

"Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand", Thoreau writes in Walden, adding "Simplify, simplify" and that one meal a day and five dishes instead of a hundred would do [3]. He saw discerning the necessary and the real as the crucial ethical task, freeing life of encumbrances as a mathematician reduces an equation [2].

Epictetus's Encheiridion opens: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion ... and in a word, whatever are our acts. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices" [3]. Treating what is not yours as yours brings hindrance and lament, while attending only to what is your own means no one can compel or harm you [3]; the Stoics focused on what is under our control, the judgment we render on our instinctive reactions [2].

In On Liberty Mill warned that when society itself is the tyrant it "practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression", since it "leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself" [1]. So protection is needed against "the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling" as well as against the magistrate [1].

Sun Tzu says knowledge of the enemy's dispositions "can only be obtained from other men", not by divination or calculation [3]: "Hence the use of spies, of whom there are five classes: local spies, inward spies, converted spies, doomed spies, surviving spies" [4]. When all five are at work "none can discover the secret system", which he calls the sovereign's most precious faculty [4].

Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay [1][2]. They hid their identities at the time, writing as "Publius" [3]; later scholarship assigns Hamilton 51 of the 85 essays, Madison 29 and Jay 5 [2].

Murasaki Shikibu, also called Lady Murasaki, a noblewoman, poet and lady-in-waiting of the Heian court, in the early 11th century [1][2]. The title page of Arthur Waley's 1925 translation gives "The Tale of Genji by Lady Murasaki" [1]; how much of the tale is hers has been debated for centuries [4].

The Rubaiyat is a collection of quatrains (rubaiyat) attributed to the Persian poet Omar Khayyam [1]. It became known to English readers through Edward FitzGerald's 1859 verse translation, "Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam ... Rendered into English Verse by Edward Fitzgerald" [1][3].

The Kalevala is "the epic poem of Finland", here in John Martin Crawford's 1888 English translation [1]. It relates the contests between the Finns and the "darksome Laplanders", read also as a contest between light and darkness, and is full of folklore about the origin of things, its heroes overcoming an evil by chanting its origin [3][4].

Exodus: the text appears at Exodus 20:1-17, and again at Deuteronomy 5:6-21, with a "Ritual Decalogue" at Exodus 34:11-26 [1]. The King James text begins "Thou shalt have no other gods before me" (20:3) [3].

Ishmael: the book opens "Call me Ishmael", a man who takes to the sea whenever he finds himself growing grim about the mouth [3]. Ralph Ellison's narrator introducing himself ("I am an invisible man") is modelled on that opening [4].

Yes, the Analects, a compilation of sayings and discussions of Confucius and his disciples, traditionally held to have been compiled by his followers [2][4]. One example: asked for one word to live by, the Master said "Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others" [1].
The Hispaniola, a two-hundred-ton schooner bought and fitted out in Bristol [1]. The story was first serialised as Treasure Island or the Mutiny of the Hispaniola [4].

Jacob Marley, who was dead when the story opens: "Marley was dead: to begin with", and Scrooge signed the burial register [1]. The story begins seven years after his death, and Marley's ghost visits Scrooge that night [2][3].

Under six inches: Gulliver, pinned to the ground in Lilliput, sees "a human creature not six inches high, with a bow and arrow in his hands" [2]. Lilliput is the land where all the people are tiny [3].

He made it look like a privilege. Faced with thirty yards of fence, Tom told Ben that Aunt Polly was "awful particular" and hardly one boy in a thousand could do it right [1][2], and the boys ended up giving him their treasures for a turn, so the fence got three coats while he idled; he had discovered that "in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain" [3].

The harpoon line catches him: after Ahab darts the harpoon the line runs foul, he clears it, "but the flying turn caught him round the neck, and voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim, he was shot out of the boat" [3]. The line loops around his neck and drags him to his death on the third day of the chase [1].
The passages give Methuselah's age, 969 years, "the longest lifespan claimed in the Bible" [1][2], but they don't give Noah's age at death, so the difference can't be worked out from them.
